scope_note: Normalized graph generated from 99 validated portable records plus every additional bundled root reader with an explicitly named local package, covering 768 distinct text layers. It carries the archive's 81-entry English EOTC list as a cited list, not as an independent canon determination. It also includes a separate transcription of the 81 numbered labels on an Eritrean Orthodox Diocese page; that page list is not an independently established synodical canon, and no EOTC–Eritrean work crosswalk is inferred. Only documented crosswalk assertions are included; unmapped identities and verse-level alignments remain unresolved. It is not a complete scripture collection, complete language coverage, or a claim that all layer texts are accurate or complete.

traditions.notes: A tradition label for the cited English list; no claim is made that the list settles all community canon usage.

labels.value: Eritrean Orthodox Tewahdo Church (as named by the cited page)

traditions.notes: The cited page is hosted by the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahdo Church Diocese of the U.S.A. and Canada. Its 81 numbered labels are transcribed as that page presents them; the page cites the Ethiopian Church list and Wikipedia. This record does not establish a synod-approved Eritrean canon or an equivalence with the Ethiopian list.

works.notes: Research corpus ID: amh2003-1co-research. scope: This is the Amharic New Testament publisher-menu entry 7 under label '1ኛ ወደ ቆሮንቶስ ሰዎች' and standard book code 1CO. The 81-entry catalogue link is provisional and title-level; relation to any particular church canon list or printed exemplar is not established. layers.notes: The eBible publisher metadata does not document a source-text path. Haile Selassie's 1961 statement describes the 1947–1952 committee's aim as revising the existing Amharic Bible with reference to Hebrew and Greek. A. F. Matthew, a committee member, reports that the 1955 New Testament revision used Nestle's 1904 Greek text, following an Ethiopic reading where the Nestle apparatus listed the same alternative. These are historical statements about the revision process, not proof that this 2003 digital witness reproduces the 1962 print text without change. No collation establishes this reader's book-level lineage, so its path remains unknown. Translation source language/path is not established in the available record.

citations.supports_claim: Inspected October 2026; the Church’s English canon page is undated. It states 81 canonized books (46 Old Testament, 35 New Testament) and gives grouped/combined titles; it names the “Book of Josephas the Son of Bengorion.” This is evidence for the Church’s stated list, not for every split display row, a modern English edition, completeness, chapter boundaries, or reuse rights. The same page’s prose outside the numbered list says the Ethiopic version includes Baruch and third and fourth Esdras, and says the Ascension of Isaiah was preserved in Ethiopic. These mentions are not separate headings in the numbered 81-entry list; their exact work identities and relationship to grouped Ezra entries are unresolved. Treat them as source-stated leads, not additional entries or verified crosswalks. Follow-up context: prose outside this page’s numbered 81-entry list also mentions Baruch and “the third and fourth Esdras,” and says the Ascension of Isaiah was preserved in Ethiopic. Those statements are not separate headings in the numbered list; keep their relationship to the grouped Ezra entries explicit and do not use them to change the 81-entry count.

The university-hosted Ethiopic Bible index lists Genesis in the Octateuch section and links its chapters. The page describes the Ge’ez text as following August Dillmann’s edition and digitized by Ran HaCohen. The archive stores all 50 chapter source pages locally. This historical edition is not identified as the current official EOTC printed edition. The same public index also visibly lists these additional Old Testament menu labels: Regum; Paralipomena (editor label Grébaut); Ezra (Pereira); Esther (Pereira); Iob (Pereira); Proverbia (Pilkington); Ecclesiastes (Mercer); Canticorum (Gleave); Isaia (Bachmann); Lamentationes (Bachmann); Daniel (Löfgren); Hosea (Fuhs); Ioel; Amos (Pereira); Abdias (Bachmann); Ionas (Löfgren); Michaeas (Fuhs); Nahum, Habacuc, Sophonias, Aggaeus, Zacharias and Malachias (Löfgren); Baruch et Epistola Jeremiae; Tobith; Judith; Siracida; Sapientia Solomonis; Ezrae Apocalypsis; Ezra Graecus; Jubilaeorum (VanderKam and a second menu entry); 4 Baruch; Henoch (three menu entries, including Flemming and Charles); Ascensio Isaiae (Charles). These are transcribed menu labels and edition credits, not verified book crosswalks or evidence of accessible/complete chapter texts. Except for the separately audited local Genesis–Ruth, Psalms, Jubilees, and 1 Enoch packages, item URLs, chapter boundaries, text extent, current availability, and item-specific reuse conditions have not been checked. Do not count a menu entry as reader coverage. Follow-up research recorded 2026-10-25: separate TAU information pages for Ezra, the Ethiopic apocrypha, and the Ascension of Isaiah now provide edition descriptions and selected chapter-access claims (SRC-097–SRC-100). They do not establish complete local chapter inventories, exact EOTC crosswalks, wording, completeness, or permission for unrestricted reuse. Rechecked 2026-10-25 against the live index: under LIBRI HISTORICI it lists ‘Paralipomena’ and credits editor Grébaut; two selection controls are visible, but their targets and contents are not audited. The index alone does not establish whether both numbered Chronicles are available, their chapter boundaries, completeness, or reuse rights. Paralipomena capture audit 2026-10-26: the two index functions now resolve to separate 29- and 36-item numbered menus, credited to Grébaut. Locally retained page-wrapper HTML confirms each menu target displays a PNG scan; no page images or OCR text are bundled. This verifies the observed menu entries and wrapper targets, not completeness of the printed edition or exact identity with a current EOTC edition. See SRC-338. Ezra follow-up (2026-10-26): the live ‘Ezra and Nehemia’ form exposes 23 menu options numbered 1–23; see SRC-361 and research/ezra-nehemia-menu-audit.json. This records menu structure only, not a page-by-page text audit or proof of completeness. Pereira structural follow-up (2026-10-26): the 1919 printed edition numbers the grouped work I–XXIII, with Ezra X ending before Nehemiah XI begins (SRC-362); TAU's 23 menu targets are consistent with this, but were not individually collated. Pereira reports manuscript chapter divisions vary, including an unchaptered witness.

Bibliographic note identifies Dillmann’s Veteris Testamenti Aethiopici Tomus Primus / Octateuchus Aethiopicus (Leipzig, 1853–1855). The digitizer reports OCR followed by proofreading/corrections, but warns new typos may remain; the critical apparatus is not included. The note says Boyd’s later 1909 edition stopped after Leviticus. Ethiopic verse numbering was replaced by Arabic numerals, follows the Septuagint, and may have discontinuities where the Ethiopic translation omits a Septuagint verse. Preserve this edition’s numbering; do not treat the transcription as freshly collated. The digitizer explains the visible editorial signs: parentheses mark Ethiopic additions to the Septuagint; square brackets mark omissions supplied according to later Ethiopic manuscripts; paired asterisks mark rare additions by Dillmann. These conventions are not a substitute for the omitted critical apparatus.

The page describes many Geʽez Old Testament books and the entire New Testament, but does not establish coverage of all 81 Church-list entries. The digitizer grants free use, copying, and distribution of the digitized Ethiopic text for noncommercial purposes if © Ran HaCohen and the permission notice accompany every copy. Other uses require contacting the copyright owner. The Genesis reader includes that notice; this is not a grant of commercial rights.

SAGE metadata identifies this peer-reviewed article in The Bible Translator 67(2), pp. 202–222, first online 14 September 2016, © author. Its abstract says the Church traditionally cites 81 books but that the composition of this list is obscure and critically discusses canon as a concept. Only publisher metadata and abstract were inspected here; full article access is restricted. This is scholarly analysis, not an official Church ruling; no article text is bundled.

The university-hosted dissertation identifies Bruk Ayele Asale as author, a PhD in New Testament (Biblical Studies), submitted to the University of KwaZulu-Natal in March 2015. Its discussion at pp. 178–180 reviews earlier scholarship on broader/narrower lists and differing title/count traditions. It enumerates four Sinodos books by the names Ser’ata Seyon (Order of Zion), Te’ezaz, Gessew, and Abtelis; it also describes two Books of the Covenant, three Epistles of Clement counted as one book, and Didascalia in a broader-list account. At printed p. 229 (PDF page 248) it says the manuscript connection between Proverbs and Tegsas is unclear. These are attributed scholarly comparisons, not an official Church ruling or proof that this Church-page label identifies the same edition or exact textual boundaries. The archive cites but does not reproduce the thesis.

SAGE metadata identifies the peer-reviewed article by G.A. Mikre-Sellassie, The Bible Translator 44/1 (January 1993), pp. 111–123. The full article PDF was inspected. On printed p. 120, note 51 reports a five-part Solomon grouping in the Amharic commentary on Fetha Negest: Messale (Proverbs 1–24), Tegsas (Proverbs 25–31), Wisdom, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Songs. Printed pp. 120–122 distinguish broader and narrower historical canon lists and describe differing enumerations; this is an attributed historical scholarly account, not an official current ruling or an edition-level crosswalk to the Church's undated English list. The article is not bundled. The separately hosted PDF is at https://translation.bible/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/mikre-sellassie-1993-the-bible-and-its-canon-in-the-ethiopian-orthodox-church.pdf.

Oxford Research Archive metadata identifies Hugh Pilkington's DPhil thesis, A critical edition of the Book of Proverbs in Ethiopic, awarded by Oxford in 1978, with two OCR PDF files and copyright metadata naming Pilkington (1978). The repository abstract states that Cambridge University Library Add. 1570 was the base text; 21 Ethiopic manuscripts and two printed sources were collated; and the base text was translated literally to retain Ethiopic idiosyncrasies. The abstract reports four textual traditions, mixed Greek and Hebraic features, and LXX-dependent chapter/verse structure. These are the thesis author's summary claims, not independently checked conclusions. A secondary index assigns a purported Book of Rebukes section to pp. 318–522, but the thesis PDFs and those pages have not been inspected here; exact Tegsats boundaries, text content, translation extent, and completeness are unverified. The repository lists copyright dated 1978 and no open license is recorded; no thesis text is copied. Inspected the repository abstract and item metadata 2026-10-26. DOI: 10.5287/ora-kzy5ayyad.

Inspected the open-access 2024 chapter. Bausi identifies the Ethiopic Maṣḥafa Qalemǝnṭos (Book of Clement; CAe 1957) as the Ethiopic version of the Arabic Apocalypse of Peter to Clement, distinguishes it from the Ethiopic Apocalypse of Peter (CAe 317), and describes a stable seven-book structure with only partial correspondence to the Arabic work. He states that no comprehensive critical edition exists; French translations cover books I–II and Italian translation covers books III–VII. He discusses an Eritrean manuscript documented in 1992 and revisited in 2019, and cautions that a recent Geʽez–Amharic printed edition is not institutionally sponsored by the EOTC, does not meet scholarly standards, and may adapt, rearrange, or rewrite its source. This is a scholarly study, not the full manuscript or a Church ruling. No text copied; manuscript completeness and the exact crosswalk to the Church website's grouped Book of Clement remain unverified. The PDF imprint states CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (noncommercial redistribution of the unaltered work with attribution); this publication license does not grant rights in the manuscript or texts it studies.

Inspected the full article text on an online host. Cowley explicitly warns that canon-list naming does not always uniquely identify a text. He reports that three Ethiopic Mäqabeyan books are counted as two in one canon-law commentary (the second and third counted together), distinguishes them from all four Septuagint Maccabees and from Pseudo-Josephus, and describes the contents of “1 Maccabees” in the Geʽez–Amharic printed Bibles cited in his notes. Footnote 7 identifies an undated four-volume London photolithographic Geʽez–Amharic Bible prepared by 1927 E.C.; its volume 3 contains 1–3 Maccabees. This is historical secondary scholarship and bibliographic reporting, not direct inspection of that edition or a Church ruling. The exact relation between that printed text, manuscript witnesses, and the current Church-list title remains uncertain. No text copied. Rechecked 2026-10-27 for the Te'ezaz lead: Cowley describes Sinodos as four apostolically attributed sections and says Te'ezaz is attested with 71 or 72 canons and was printed in Horner's 1904 Statutes (footnote 12). The main index form titled ‘The Apocalypse of Esdras (2 Esdras)’ and labeled ‘Ezrae Apocalypsis’ lists menu labels 1–14 with image-page targets Apocryphi/Apop 153.html, 155, 158, 161, 164, 166, 170, 172, 175, 177, 181, 183, 186, and 189; a plus-sign target at 192 follows. The linked HTML pages display scanned page images, not a parsed transcription. This menu inventory confirms access points only; it does not independently establish that each is a chapter boundary, all pages of each chapter, complete book scope, exact current-edition identity, or textual accuracy. No pages or text are bundled.

This project report says its group acquired a printed book it calls Josippon/Yosëf wäldä Koryonor, The Book of Josephas the Son of Ben Gorion, and Zëna Ayhud. It says the title page reads Zëna Ayhud in Amharic and the project identifies the volume as the right work from the greater EOTC canon. This is the project's own report and identification, not an EOTC-issued catalogue record, bibliographic edition record, or independent text collation. The post does not give a publisher, publication date, full edition statement, or reusable full text; no text or image is copied here. The page carries a 2017–2026 copyright notice. Inspected 2026-10-26.

Inspected the 2012 PhD thesis awarded by the University of St. Michael's College, Toronto School of Theology. On printed p. 29, Gebru describes the Ethiopic Didascalia as a 43-chapter work, says chapters 1–32 correspond with variations to the 27 chapters of the Syriac Didascalia Apostolorum, and describes chapters 33–43 as material from Books VI–VII of the Apostolic Constitutions, including an abridged Book VII sequence with a reported omission. Gebru reviews competing scholarly accounts of the Ethiopic work's textual ancestry and suggests an Arabic basis; this is attributed scholarly interpretation, not a settled or independently verified stemma. The thesis states that Harden's 1920 translation is complete and Platt's 1834 translation contains only the first 23 chapters. These are secondary scholarly claims about those editions, not a local collation of either scan or proof of the Church-list entry's exact boundaries. No thesis text or scripture text is copied into the archive. Inspected 2026-10-26.

Inspected 2026-10-27 from a commit-pinned GitHub raw TEI file (commit 330a89d34e4088d2eaabb5b87101dbf054457166; 16,865 bytes; SHA-256 db5f90e9b78079a7befae9a7a081ec72c10c1bedfaef79ef847d3f466796dd6e). Its title statement gives Geʽez, normalized, and English title forms for Maṣḥafa Qalemǝnṭos / Book of Clement. The TEI text section has an introduction, seven numbered Book divisions, and short Geʽez incipit divisions; no chapter/verse hierarchy or continuous full book text was found. The file itself states CC BY-SA 4.0. Beta maṣāḥǝft's current Guidelines state CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for project data/remixes, while the University of Hamburg dataset record carries dataset-level CC BY 4.0 metadata and defers to file-level notices. Because the terms differ and no text is bundled, reuse of the transcription remains unresolved. The work record identifies CAe 1957; it does not prove identity with the exact Church-list entry. See local metadata-only capture and review.

Inspected 2026-10-26. eBible.org identifies the English, British/International WEBBE 2020 stable text edition, labels it public domain, and offers USFM. The stored package and its signed checksum list are retained locally. This is source-edition evidence, not EOTC/Eritrean canon evidence or independent translation-accuracy evidence.

eBible.org states that WEBBE is public domain and that the name is trademarked. The provider asks that if actual text or punctuation is changed, the result not be called the World English Bible. The exact signed source package is preserved; the reader view is a normalized extraction.

The provider says WEBBE is WEBU with British/International spelling; describes the broader WEB revision as an ASV update with New Testament conformity to Greek Majority Text where significant differences occur; and says WEB Apocrypha/Deuterocanon comes from Revised Version 1894 or LXX2012 where needed. These are edition-family statements, not a verified path for each bundled module.

Package SHA-256 54ec9e6b277c95c20ac173927fa7a976f37d86f0c0a54f132ba9f6666d93b6f6; 87 ZIP members; 81 scripture modules, one preface, one glossary, and supporting files. GnuPG reports a good signature from the co-distributed key claiming World English Bible editors (54D714D76956DA6673DC1EEA5F62009D93505F26), but trust is undefined and signing authority was not independently authenticated. All ordinary member hashes match the signed list.

The archive authority record labels John Mason Harden's dates as 1871–1931 and describes his education and church career. The record is marked preliminary and minimum detail, and it cites Eduardo Henriques Moreira (1949) as a source. The name and dates are a biographical lead for the J. M. Harden credited in the 1920 Didascalia edition; this record alone does not establish that identity or determine copyright status in any jurisdiction. The page's notice restricts reuse of its text and images; no image or extended text is copied here. Inspected 2026-10-26.

The record describes The Wonderful and Most Deplorable History of the Later Times of the Jews, an English edition with a 1718 title page and a 1722 advertisement. Its edition note identifies Peter Morwen's English as a translation of Abraham ben David ibn Daud's abstract of book 3 of Sefer ha-kabalah, an abridgement associated with Josippon and historically attributed to Joseph ben Gorion/Josephus. This is a bibliographic record, not a checked copy or text; it is not a full English translation of the Ethiopic Church-list work. No text or images copied. Inspected 2026-10-26.

This bibliography records the Boston English edition as 1718 [i.e. 1722?], 332 pages, and identifies Peter Morwen as the unnamed translator based on the Dictionary of National Biography. It independently documents the edition bibliographically, not its textual extent relative to the Ethiopic work. No text copied. Inspected 2026-10-26.

The publisher describes an English print edition and calls its Josippon a documented reconstruction of about 116 chapters / 41,000 words, not a direct Geʽez translation. Its stated method uses Latin translations of Hebrew Sefer Yosippon, a chapter mapping attributed to Yonatan Binyam's 2017 dissertation, and E. A. Wallis Budge's translation for one Alexander section. These are publisher statements, not independently checked against the print copy, source-language text, dissertation chart, or full chapter inventory. The site carries a © 2026 notice; no reuse license for the full edition was found. No text copied. Inspected 2026-10-26.

JSTOR identifies this as a free 12-page article in Journal of the Society of Biblical Literature and Exegesis 5, no. 1/2 (1885), pp. 61–72. The article states that Schodde translated the Ethiopic Canons using Fell’s 1871 edition, which includes a Latin version. The bundled 13-page PDF contains one repository notice followed by the 12 printed article pages. A visual audit inventories all 57 printed headings I–LVII on PDF pages 4–13 (printed pages 63–72); it verifies labels and locations only. The opening formula and Canons I–LVII except Canon XX were transcribed against the scan; Canon XX is visibly cut off after ‘from me,’ on printed page 65, and the text-layer reading ‘I Peter’ is not visible in this scan. Remaining wording has not been proofread. A page-labeled pypdf text-layer extraction is bundled as raw research data only; it is not a verified transcript or reader. A separate partial transcription of the opening formula and Canons I–LVII was visually proofread against the scan, except Canon XX which is recorded only as a visible fragment. The remaining unproofread material is the article introduction and footnotes. A second online PDF copy from biblicalstudies.org.uk was downloaded and had the same SHA-256 as the bundled scan; it is not an independent witness and does not resolve the visible Canon XX gap. The partial work is not a complete reader and does not increase reader coverage. JSTOR states that, to its knowledge, the journal issue is in the public domain and may be used accordingly. This does not establish accuracy or equivalence to every Ethiopic Sinodos manuscript or modern Church edition.

Inspected 2026-10-27. The publisher states that WEB is based on the American Standard Version (1901), Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia Old Testament, and a combination of original ASV source-text choices and the Greek Majority Text New Testament. It says WEBBE uses British spelling and LORD/GOD renderings. It separately states that the Deuterocanon/Apocrypha companion derives from the Revised Version Apocrypha and Brenton's English Septuagint translation. These are publisher descriptions of edition lineage, not per-module textual collation or independent accuracy findings.

Inspected 2026-10-27. At printed p. 120, Mikre-Sellassie describes Sinodos as four sections and reports Te'ezaz as containing 71 canons, citing G. Horner, The Statutes of the Apostles (1904), in footnote 47. This independently supports the section's title/count connection to Horner, but is secondary scholarship, not a direct Church ruling or manuscript collation. The article itself discusses broader/narrower canon lists and unresolved counting differences elsewhere; it must not be used to assert one universally settled canon form. No text copied.
